The truth value of a compound proposition depends upon the truth values of its component atomic propositions.
All non-atomic propositions are compound propositions.

For example: ‘I am a student at university, and I am studying for a maths degree’ is a compound proposition. It is constructed from two atomic propositions: ‘I am a student at university’ and ‘I am studying for a maths degree’.

In addition to the three basic logical connectives AND, OR and NOT, there are two
implication connectives, Conditional and Biconditional.
2.2.4 Conditional or Implication proposition
In logical arguments the ‘If … then’ construct or relationship is very often used.
Conditional constructions are particularly used in programming for loop control and
in branching.
For two propositions p and q, the conditional if p then q symbolically is denoted as
p q or p → q and is frequently read “ p implies q” or “p only if q”.
In the conditional statement p → q, p is called the hypothesis (or antecedent or premise)
and q is called the conclusion (or consequence).
The truth table for the conditional (or implication) of two simple propositions p and q is
given by

2.2.5 Biconditional or Equivalence
For two propositions p and q, the compound proposition ‘p if and only if q, or
p iff q’ is referred to as the biconditional statement and symbolically is denoted as
p q.
The truth table for the biconditional or equivalence of two propositions p and q is given
by:
p q p q
T T T
T F F
F T F
F F T
We can think of “p q” as follows:

p if and only if q.
For p to be true, it is necessary and sufficient for q to be true.
p implies q and q implies p.
p is equivalent to q.
A biconditional proposition “p if and only if q” involves two conditional propositions,
“If p, then q” and “If q, then p”.
Thus, p q is true whenever p and q have the same truth values.
Note that p q is equivalent to (p q)  (q p); This can be shown by using truth
tables.

the truth value of the resulting expression. That is the truth value of pq is the same as
the truth value of q p. The connective  is not symmetric: p  q and q  p have
